newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Brazil ready for re-election battle.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Brazil ready for re-election battle.

text.p: One question is going to dominate Brazilian politics in the coming months -- will President Fernando Henrique Cardoso emulate his Argentine and Peruvian counterparts and win a chance for a second term?

Cardoso's dream of being the first Brazilian president ever to be re-elected was Brasilia's worst kept secret until he confirmed recently that he wants to be Brazil's first reelected president. "I am in favour of re-election as an idea and if the constitution were to be rewritten I think I should have the right to stand," he said in a newspaper interview.

With high personal approval ratings and the "Real Plan," which stopped raging inflation, still popular, he would be hard to beat in 1998. But he is barred from re-election by the constitution, which restricts holders of executive office -- presidents, governors and mayors -- to one term.

Hardly a day goes by without a soap opera actress, an Olympic athlete or a visiting head of state emerging from the presidential office to tell reporters how wonderful four more Cardoso years would be. Government ministers and markets are also arguing ever more fervently that Brazil needs the continuity of another Cardoso term to build on newfound economic stability begun in July 1994 with the Real Plan.

The plan, dreamed up by Cardoso when he was finance minister in the government of President Itamar Franco, introduced a new currency, the real, which was tied loosely to the dollar, and did away with automatic, monthly wage and price increases that for years had fuelled inflation. As a result, inflation has fallen to below 0.5 percent a month, down from an annualized 5,000 percent in June 1994.

Cardoso, if he remains in office until 2002, would seek to deepen his government reforms, which have been modest so far, dismantle Brazil's restrictive labour laws, improve its crumbling roads, ports and railways, and press ahead with regional and global trade agreements, analysts say.

"There can be no economic stability without political stability," said parliamentary deputy Jose Mendonca Filho, whose bill to rewrite the constitution and allow re-election has been gathering dust in Congress for a year and a half.

Committee-level debate is expected to begin in mid-October and government whips are rolling up their sleeves for what is likely to prove the Cardoso administration's biggest challenge to date in the volatile Chamber of Deputies.
"There's nothing on the agenda other than re-election. All the other reforms have been forgotten about for now," said Dora Kramer, the doyenne of Brasilia's political columnists.

Rewriting the constitution is no easy task. The government took nearly a year to get a package of pension reforms through committees only to see it rendered meaningless on the floor of the lower house of parliament. But the re-election issue is unlikely to prove so prickly because, unlike pension reform, it does not threaten the perks of deputies and the public sector lobbies they defend, political analysts said.

But it will openly pit Cardoso's presidential ambitions against those of rivals from other parties whose backing he needs. The real battle will be in the lower house, the Chamber of Deputies, where constitutional amendments need two three-fifths majorities, each equivalent to 308 votes.

Cardoso himself, in an interview with Jornal do Brasil's Kramer on the eve of elections in 1994, said re-election would prove too hot an issue to touch during his term. "In a country like this, imagine what a campaign for re-electing a sitting president would be like. He is liable to lose everything because everyone will say he is using the state machine to get what he wants," he was quoted as saying.

For years, the idea of re-election has been a taboo that smacks of the country's authoritarian past under the Portuguese and the 1964-85 military dictatorship. In a recent poll, only 38 percent of deputies backed giving Cardoso the chance to run in 1998, but nearly 70 percent supported the idea for future presidents, governors and mayors, giving whips a wide field for negotiating support.

"Half of those who say they back the concept of re-election could be persuaded to extend it to Fernando Henrique with just a few telephone calls from the president," said political analyst Murillo Aragao.
And a cabinet reshuffle is reported to be in the pipeline to reward allies for their support in the re-election battle.

While Cardoso's Brazilian Social Democratic Party and his staunch allies in the Liberal Front Party will vote in favour of re-election, fur will fly in the scramble for the votes of the 89 deputies of the Brazilian Progressive Party.

The PPB is the party of Paulo Maluf, outgoing mayor of Sao Paulo, whose burning presidential ambitions and sway over PPB deputies would get a big boost if Celso Pitta, his would-be successor, wins the Sao Paulo mayoral race, as expected. A first round of municipal elections takes place on Oct. 3, followed by a second round on Nov. 15 in big city elections not already won by outright majorities.
"Maluf is red hot for the presidency. If he elects his successor, the next day he will begin his campaign for 1998," Brasilia University politics professor David Fleischer said.
